summary: Explores what a host could do when it gets an ICMP source quench message. It proposes that each source host's IP module add some delay between datagrams sent to the same destination. The authors call it a "crazy idea paper" meant to start discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router is overloaded it drops packets and sends a message back to the sender saying so. This RFC asks what the sender should do about it. The answer it proposes is simple: the sending machine keeps a small delay for each destination, adds to it when a complaint arrives, and takes it away again very slowly. The machine therefore spreads its packets out instead of firing them off in bursts.

questions: what can a host do with a source quench
how does source quench congestion control work
subtitle: A 1987 idea paper on slowing a host down when a gateway says the network is full.

tldr.problem: When a gateway runs out of buffer space it throws datagrams away and sends a source quench back to the sender, asking it to slow down. IP has no agreed way to act on that request, and the layer above usually never hears about it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes that the sending IP module keep a per-destination delay. On receiving a quench it raises the delay by a fixed step, and it lowers the delay again very slowly, so that the sending rate creeps back up until the network complains once more.
tldr.outcome: The document calls itself a crazy idea paper and asks for discussion. It reports a simulation in which a host that spaces its datagrams out achieves better throughput than one that does not.

facts.label: Queue levels in the test model
facts.value: Quenches from 70 percent, discards from 95 percent, stop at 50 percent

today: RFC 1016 was published in July 1987 as a discussion paper, and it describes itself as a crazy idea paper for which discussion is essential. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Source Quench and What It Means
sections.content:
A gateway may discard Internet datagrams if it does not have the buffer space needed to queue them for output to the next network on the route to the destination. If a gateway discards a datagram, it may send a source quench message to the Internet source host of the datagram. A destination host may also send a source quench message if datagrams arrive too fast to be processed. The source quench message is a request to the host to cut back the rate at which it is sending traffic to the Internet destination, and the gateway may send one for every message it discards.

On receipt of a source quench, the source host should cut back the rate at which it sends traffic to the specified destination until it no longer receives source quench messages from the gateway. It can then gradually increase the rate at which it sends traffic to the destination until it again receives source quench messages. The gateway or host may send the source quench message when it approaches its capacity limit rather than waiting until the capacity is exceeded, which means that the data datagram which triggered the source quench message may still be delivered.

The status of the document is unusual and is stated at the top. The memo is intended to explore the issue of what a host could do with a source quench, and the proposal is for each source host IP module to introduce some delay between datagrams sent to the same destination host. It describes itself as a crazy idea paper, and says that discussion is essential.
sections.plainLanguage: A source quench is a router saying, in effect, that you are sending too fast. The RFC notes that the router may send it before it starts dropping packets, so the packet that triggered the complaint may still get through. The idea is to treat the complaint as a signal to slow down, rather than as an error to be ignored.

sections.title: The SQuID Concept
sections.content:
Suppose the IP module at the datagram source has a queue of datagrams to send, and the IP module has a parameter D. D is the introduced delay between sending datagrams from the queue to the network. That is, when the IP module discovers a datagram waiting to be sent to the network, it sends it to the network and then waits time D before even looking at the datagram queue again. Normally, the value of D is zero.

The proposal is that when a source quench is received, or any other signal is received that the host should slow down its transmissions to the network, the value of D is increased, and that as time goes by the value of D is decreased. That is the whole of the concept: a delay that grows when the network complains and shrinks again slowly when it stops complaining.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is one number per destination. The number is a pause. After sending a packet to that destination the machine waits that long before looking at its queue again. Normally the pause is zero, so nothing changes for a well-behaved network.

sections.title: The Algorithm and How to Implement It
sections.content:
The algorithm is given as two rules. On an increase event, D is set to the maximum of D plus K and I, where K is 0.020 second and I is 0.075 second. On a decrease event, D is set to the maximum of D minus J and zero, where J is 0.001 second. An increase event is the receipt of one or more source quenches in an event period E, where E is 2.000 seconds. A decrease event is when S time has passed since D was decreased and there is a datagram to send, where S is 1.000 second. A cache of D values is kept for the last M hosts communicated with. The RFC notes that when no datagrams are sent to a destination for some time, the D for that destination is not decreased, but that if a destination is not used for a long time, its D may fall out of the cache.

The implementation must keep the state small. Since IP does not normally keep much state information about things, the authors want the default or idle IP to have no state about these D values, so IP should keep a list only of those destinations with non-zero D values. When IP wants to send a datagram it searches the list to see whether the destination is noted; if it is not, the D value is zero and the datagram is sent at once. If the destination is listed, IP must wait the indicated D time before sending that particular datagram, though it could look at a datagram addressed to a different destination and possibly send that in the meantime. When IP receives a source quench it checks whether the destination in the datagram that caused it is on the list; if so it adds K to the D value, and if not it appends the destination to the list with the D value set to I.

The RFC lists possible refinements. Keep a separate outgoing queue of datagrams for each destination host, local subnet or network. Keep the cache of D values per network or local subnet instead of per host. Make I based on the basic speed of the slowest intervening network. Limit D so that it never goes below I if that refinement is implemented. Make S based on the round trip time. Adjust D datagram by datagram according to the length of the datagrams, waiting longer after a long datagram. Or implement the delay so that if a source does not send a datagram when it is next allowed, it gets a credit for one and only one free, no-delay, datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: The pause grows by twenty milliseconds at a time and never falls below seventy-five milliseconds. It shrinks by one millisecond at a time, and only when there is something to send. A burst of complaints counts as one event, so the pause does not leap up when a router complains about every dropped packet. The list of paused destinations is kept only for those that currently have a pause, so a quiet machine keeps no state at all.

sections.title: What the Gateway Should Do
sections.content:
For the algorithm to work the authors rely on gateways sending source quenches to say how things are going. Because the loss of a single datagram affects data flow so much, it would be much better for the source IP node if it got a warning before datagrams were discarded.

The proposal is that gateway IP nodes start sending source quenches before the node is flooded, at a level called SQ Keep, but still forward the datagram. If the queue level reaches a critical level, SQ Toss, the gateway should toss datagrams to resolve the problem, unless the datagram is an ICMP message; even ICMP messages are tossed if the MaxQ level is reached. Once the gateway starts sending quenches it should continue to do so until the queue level goes below a low water mark, SQLW, which the RFC calls analogous to methods some operating systems use for memory space management. The gateway should try to send a quench to as many of the contributors to the congestion as possible, but only once per contributor per second or two.
sections.plainLanguage: The router side is a set of queue levels. At seventy percent full the router starts complaining but keeps forwarding; at ninety-five percent it starts throwing packets away; and it keeps complaining until the queue drains back to fifty percent. The effect is a warning that arrives before the damage.

sections.title: The Test Model
sections.content:
To test the algorithm and its parameters, the authors needed to check the interaction between IP with the SQuID algorithm and TCP, and to try various combinations of retransmission strategy and source quench strategy, which required control of the entire test network. They therefore decided to build an Internet model. A program written in C created queues and structures representing datagrams carrying data, acknowledgements and source quenches, and moved datagrams from one queue to the next based on defined rules.

The example configuration is a client running TCP/IP on a 10 Mb/s LAN, an IP node, a 56 kb/s WAN link, another IP node, and a second client on a 10 Mb/s LAN. A client fed the TCP in node 1 data at the rate it would accept, and the TCP function chopped the data into fixed 512 byte datagrams, timestamping each one as it was handed to IP and keeping a copy on a TCP acknowledgement-wait queue. Each IP node had one queue in each direction, and would forward datagrams at the rate of the communications line going to the next node, so the fifth datagram on node 2's rightward queue would take 5 times 73 msec, or 365 msec, to appear at the end of node 3's queue.

The gateway source quench algorithm was modelled as well: when a datagram was put on an IP queue the number on the queue was compared to an SQ keep level, and if it was greater a source quench was generated and returned to the sender; if it was larger than the SQ toss level it was also discarded. Once quenches were generated they continued until the queue level went below the SQ low water level. The percentages were modifiable, as were many parameters, and a source quench could be lost if it exceeded the maximum queue size, though a source quench was never sent about tossing a source quench.

Some parameters used were a maximum queue length of 15 datagrams per IP direction, quenches starting at 70 percent full, data datagrams tossed but not quench datagrams at 95 percent, and quenches stopping at 50 percent. The loss rate could be set as a number of losses out of a number of datagrams sent, and a single datagram loss rate of 1 lost datagram per 300 datagrams sent was used for much of the testing. The TCP retransmission timer algorithm used an Alpha of 0.15 and a Beta of 1.5. The model did not fragment datagrams and did not implement the time-to-live function.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors wrote a simulation of a small network: two machines, a fast local network on each side, and a slow link between them, with a router in the middle. The model included TCP with a real window and retransmission timer, so that the effect of spacing out packets could be measured rather than guessed.

sections.title: What the Tests Showed
sections.content:
The results are reported with a candour the authors do not hide. All of the algorithms oscillate, some worse than others, and if just the right amount of introduced delay is used the best throughput seems to be obtained, but finding the right amount is not easy.

Throughput is adversely affected, heavily, by a single lost datagram, at least for a short time. The RFC works through the case: a window 35 datagrams wide, an average round trip delay of 2500 msec, 512 byte datagrams, and one datagram lost at the beginning. Thirty-five datagrams are given by TCP to IP and a timer is started on the first; since the first is missing the receiving TCP sends no acknowledgement but buffers the other 34 out-of-sequence datagrams. After 1.5 times 2500 msec, or 3750 msec, the datagram times out and is resent, and it arrives and is acknowledged, along with the other 34, 2500 msec later. Before the loss the sender might have been sending at the rate a 56 kb/s line could accept, about one every 75 msec; after the loss it sends at the rate of one in 6250 msec, over 83 times slower.

When a source quench does not always cause datagram loss, the sender continues to send too fast and the queue size oscillates a lot. It is important for the quench to feed back into the sending system as soon as possible, so when the source host IP receives a quench it must adjust the send rate for the datagrams still on the send queue, not just for datagrams IP is asked to send after the quench.

Window size affects the chance of getting a quench. In the model, with a queue level of 15 for node 2 and a window of 20 datagrams, a burst of 20 datagrams reaches node 2 in 81 msec while the transition from node 2 to node 3 takes 73 msec, so only one datagram is forwarded and the 17th to 20th are lost every time a whole window is sent. If the window is smaller than the maximum queue size in the bottleneck node, sending a window's worth of data is done independently of the current queue size, so the larger the window the larger a percentage of the stressed queue is sent.

The RFC concludes that it seems as though in a race between a TCP session that delays sending to IP and one that does not, the delayer gets better throughput because fewer datagrams are lost. If gateways send quenches early, do not toss data until it is critical, and keep sending quenches until a low water mark is hit, effective throughput goes up. The document also notes that a large part of the perceived round trip time is due to the delay getting off the queue between TCP and IP, and that if IP invoked back-pressure on TCP in a real implementation this could be significantly reduced. It finishes with the authors' wider thoughts, including the observation that any fix must be implementable piecemeal, and that the SQuID algorithm could be installed in one location and used effectively, and the suggestion, attributed to John Nagle, that congestion should be pushed out to the edges of the network and the interior kept uncongested.
sections.plainLanguage: The honest summary is that every version of the scheme oscillates, and that getting the delay right is the hard part. The measurements do show that spacing packets out beats firing them in bursts, and that warning a sender before dropping its packets makes the whole path faster. The RFC also points out that a single lost packet can cost far more than any of the delay the scheme adds.

data.title: SQuID
data.code:
on increase event:
       D <-- maximum (D + K, I)
                          (where K = .020 second,
                                 I = .075 second)

  on decrease event:
       D <-- maximum (D - J, 0)
                          (where J = .001 second)

items.label: 0.020 second
items.desc: Added to D when an increase event occurs.

items.label: 0.075 second
items.desc: The floor for D, and the value D is set to when a destination is first listed.

items.label: 0.001 second
items.desc: Subtracted from D when a decrease event occurs, down to zero.

items.label: 2.000 seconds
items.desc: The event period: one or more quenches inside it count as a single increase event.

items.label: 1.000 second
items.desc: The interval after which D may be decreased, provided there is a datagram to send.

items.label: The last M hosts
items.desc: The number of destinations whose D values are cached.

viz.caption: THE GATEWAY QUEUE LEVELS, FROM THE TOP DOWN

layers.label: MaxQ
layers.detail: The queue is full. Datagrams are tossed and quenches sent, including ICMP messages.

layers.label: SQK, 70 percent
layers.detail: Datagrams are quenched but still forwarded.

layers.label: SQLW, 50 percent
layers.detail: Quenches stop here. The queue must fall below this level before they resume.
